title: The cell grows sweet (I.20)
hookLine: love solitude and silence; the cell often kept becomes sweet
tomorrow: if everyone carries sorrow, why does everyone else look fine?

lines: A SHUT DOOR ON A SATURDAY.
cards: A bedroom on a Saturday, door shut. No plans, no game, phone face down. To some people that's a reset.

To others it looks like hiding. The Imitation takes a side, and makes a promise: a small room, kept often, grows sweet. In a monastery that room is called a cell, a monk's or a nun's bed, desk and window.
Nothing happens there. That, the book says, is the point. But not every Catholic voice puts the weight in the same place.

teach.b: First, the case for the cell. Chapter twenty of book one says: look for a fitting time to be alone, and think often about God's kindness.
It's easier to keep quiet altogether, it says, than not to say too much, and easier to stay home than to guard yourself out in the world. Jesus gives the same gesture in Matthew.
In the Douay-Rheims: "enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father in secret." Then the promise: the cell, kept often, grows sweet; kept badly, it breeds weariness.
A room you come back to stops being empty and becomes a friend. Now the other view, and it's Catholic too. Other saints went out the door instead: to the sick, the poor, the classroom, the street.

teach.h: KEPT FOR GOD, NOT FOR ESCAPE.
teach.b: In the same Gospel, Jesus says that whatever is done for the least of his brothers is done for him. On that reading, service is its own kind of prayer, and a shut door can turn into a hiding place.
Some readers hear the Imitation as a book for monks and want it balanced by the works of mercy. The Church keeps both: communities that stay in and pray, and communities that go out and serve.
And the Imitation's own promise carries a quiet condition.
The cell grows sweet when it's kept for God, not for escape.

how: Monks and nuns in contemplative orders keep times of silence and spend time in their cells for prayer and reading, while active orders serve in schools, hospitals and parishes; lay Catholics often keep a prayer corner at home or make silent retreats.

games.q: what does “the cell grows sweet” mean?
o: a prison room gets easier to bear with time
a sweet treat saved for the hardest day
a quiet place, kept often, becomes a friend

games.q: the cell and the open door — tap the pairs.
p: a monk's or nun's small room
shut the door, pray in secret
done for the least, done for him

s: a monk's cell is a kind of prison room
it's a monk's or nun's small room: bed, desk, window, a door that closes.
the Imitation says it's easier to keep quiet altogether than to say just enough
and easier to stay home than to guard yourself well out in the world.
the Catholic Church honors only the quiet, hidden life
it keeps both: communities that stay in and pray, and communities that go out and serve.

games.q: your friend says a silent retreat weekend is selfish when the food bank needs volunteers. what's the strongest case for her side?
o: what's done for the least is done for Christ, so service can be prayer too.
retreats are boring, so volunteering is simply more fun.
silence has never helped anybody do anything good.
games.why: that's the other view at its best, and it's Catholic too. the Church keeps both the cell and the open door.

practice: Choose one quiet spot you could come back to, a chair, a corner, a window, and sit there now with your phone in another room.
Listen for the smallest sound in it, a fan, a bird, the house settling, and stay with that one sound, even when nothing else happens. If you pray, you can let the shut door be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: The cell grows sweet. The Imitation's promise for a quiet place: kept often, it turns from empty to friendly.

orig.note: Latin: the cell kept continually grows sweet; the Imitation's line in its chapter on solitude and silence.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: the cell grows sweet, and it's sweetest when you come back out kinder. Rest well.
